sites.componentType: Mine / Mill Complex
sites.componentDetail: Atlas Mine workings and the associated Atlas stamp-mill ruins near Sneffels form one historic mining-and-processing complex; keep the neighboring Revenue–Virginius property separate.
overview: The Atlas Mine and its stamp mill were part of the Sneffels mining district above Canyon Creek in Ouray County. The operation was established during the first major wave of mining development in the district in 1876 and produced precious-metal ore that was processed at the associated mill.

Federal geologic reporting documented active work at the Atlas in 1913 and examined the Klondike vein at depths ranging from roughly 850 to 1,500 feet. The surviving mill site and tailings remain the most visible historic features of the complex.

timeline.text: The Atlas operation was established during the early development of the Sneffels mining district.
U.S. Geological Survey field work documented active mining on the Klondike vein at the Atlas Mine at depths of about 850 to 1,500 feet.
The Atlas stamp mill was an important early producer in the Sneffels district and processed ore from the mine complex.
Abandoned-mine reclamation work has addressed portions of the Atlas mill and tailings area, so present-day landforms should not be assumed to match the operating-era site exactly.

moreHistory: The Atlas was one of a number of mines developed around Sneffels in the upper Canyon Creek drainage. Its mine workings and processing mill should be interpreted together as a linked industrial complex rather than as unrelated locations.
Remnant uses the historic Atlas mine locality as the identification anchor for the complex. The coordinate is a site-level historic reference, not a field survey of a safe or accessible mine opening.
Do not enter mine workings or climb on mill ruins, machinery remnants, tailings, or unstable slopes. Historic mining features in the area may be altered by weather, avalanches, and reclamation.

sites.name: Bachelor–Syracuse Mine Tour
sites.location: Gold Hill north of Ouray, Ouray County
sites.componentType: Mine
overview: The Bachelor–Syracuse is a historic precious-metal mine on Gold Hill north of Ouray. The modern visitor entrance uses the lower Syracuse Level, one part of a larger Bachelor mining system that also included older upper workings and the nearby mining settlement known as Ash.

timeline.text: Historical references place the beginning of the Bachelor Mine in the 1880s. Charlie Armstrong, George Hurlburt, and J. Frank Sanders were early owners, and rich ore supported intensive development even through the silver-price collapse of 1893.
Investors from Syracuse, New York financed the lower Syracuse Level. The tunnel became an important producing and access working and later became the underground route used for public mine tours.
Federal Defense Minerals Administration records list the Bachelor Mine in Ouray County as a lead-zinc, silver, gold, and copper property under Bachelor Development Company.
The property has continued as a tourist mine. Colorado mining regulators have documented the Bachelor Mine as an underground operation that also supports public mine tours.

moreHistory: The Bachelor property was more than one opening. Ore from the upper mine moved down Red Canyon toward Bachelor Switch, while the settlement of Ash developed near the mine with a mill, school, post office, and band. The lower Syracuse Level is a distinct component of that larger system and is the most appropriate visitor-facing identification point for the modern Bachelor–Syracuse Mine Tour. Published sources disagree on the exact discovery year, so this record does not assign a more precise origin date than the 1880s.

timeline.text: The earliest claims later incorporated into the Camp Bird property were staked.

A long aerial tram was built to move ore from the high mine to a lower stamp mill.
A fire destroyed the mill and a larger replacement followed.
A long haulage and drainage tunnel linked deep workings to the mill.
A 500-ton-per-day mill was completed during a later modernization period.
Regular mining operations ceased after decades of intermittent production and redevelopment.

Mining intensified in the late 1870s and 1880s around rich breccia-pipe, chimney, and vein deposits carrying silver, gold, lead, zinc, and copper.

Mining began in the 1870s, and Albert Reynolds later developed the long Revenue Tunnel so ore from the Virginius system could move by gravity toward the mill rather than being hoisted entirely through the upper workings.

overview: Sneffels—also known historically as Mount Sneffels and, in early accounts, Porters—was a high-elevation mining and milling settlement serving the Sneffels district southwest of Ouray.
The camp developed in the mid-1870s, received a post office under the name Mount Sneffels in 1879, and was renamed Sneffels in 1895.

moreHistory: Its importance increased when construction of the Revenue Tunnel and mill concentrated freight, workers, supplies, and ore processing in the valley.
Historic photographs document a compact settlement of log and frame buildings, a store and post office, livery and freight activity, worker housing, and major mill structures nearby.
Mining and milling contraction eventually removed most of that built environment.

Current identification should rely on the broader townsite landscape—foundations, scattered ruins, road and creek relationships, and the immediately adjacent mining-industrial setting—rather than implying that all photographed buildings survive.

Component safeguard: keep the Sneffels townsite distinct from the Revenue–Virginius and Atlas mine-and-mill complexes; treat individual commercial, residential, freight, and post-office structures as subordinate townsite components unless future expansion warrants separate records.

overview: The American Lead and Zinc Mill was a historic ore-processing site north of Ouray on the east side of the Uncompahgre River. Federal environmental records document that a mill was built and began operating here in 1930 and ceased operations in 1952.

The mill stood on a topographic bench roughly 500 feet above the river. Milling tailings were deposited in nearby ravines and on the bench, and the former mill area later became the subject of federal cleanup actions.

moreHistory: EPA records place the former mill on the east side of the Uncompahgre River roughly 2.5 miles north of downtown Ouray and describe tailings disposal in ravines near the mill and across the topographic bench.

The site is separately retained in USGS-derived topographic place records as American Lead and Zinc Mill on the Ouray quadrangle, supporting a distinct mill-site identity rather than a nearby mine record.
EPA's Superfund site database identifies American Lead and Zinc Mill in Ouray County under site ID CON000802649; it is not listed on the National Priorities List.
